stem: The passage ends with a claim. Which finding, if true, would make that claim more likely to be true?
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a Bronze Age settlement found more than two hundred clay loom weights in one building. Loom weights hold threads tight on an upright loom while cloth is woven. Very few loom weights turned up anywhere else on the site. Archaeologist Ana Reyes concludes that the building was used mainly for weaving cloth.
choices: The building had thicker stone walls than any other structure in the settlement.
Loom weights were found in roughly equal numbers in every house in the settlement.
Scraps of woven cloth and bone weaving tools lay on the building's floor near the weights.
The settlement traded its cloth with towns that were hundreds of miles away.
explanation: Start by saying the claim in your own words: this building was mainly a place for weaving. Then ask of each choice, "If this were true, would I believe that more?" Scraps of cloth and weaving tools on the same floor as the loom weights are more signs of weaving in that room, so they make the claim more likely. This is the basic move behind every "Which finding, if true, would most directly support..." question: test each choice against the exact claim, not just the topic.

A.why: This is a true-sounding fact about the right building, but thick walls say nothing about what people did inside. You matched the topic, not the claim.

B.why: The passage says very few loom weights were found elsewhere. If every house had as many, this building would not stand out, so the choice works against the claim.

D.why: Trading cloth far away is a bigger claim about the whole settlement's economy. It doesn't show what this one building was used for, so it supports a neighbouring idea instead of the claim.

stem: The passage ends with a claim. Which finding, if true, would make that claim more likely to be true?
stimulus: In 2019 the city of Halverton added protected bike lanes along Main Street. A row of concrete planters now separates cyclists from car traffic for the full length of the street. City planner Joel Okafor claims that the protected lanes have made Main Street safer for cyclists.
choices: Bicycle crashes on Main Street fell by half in the two years after the lanes opened.
The planters along Main Street were filled with flowers that are native to the region.
Bicycle crashes on Main Street doubled in the two years after the lanes opened.
Cyclists in every city across the state report feeling safer now than they did in 2019.
explanation: The claim in your own words: Main Street got safer for cyclists after the lanes went in. The key word is "safer." Fewer bicycle crashes on that street after the lanes opened is direct evidence of exactly that. Real "if true, supports" questions depend on this habit: pin down the claim's key word, then find the choice that bears on it directly.

B.why: This detail is about the right planters on the right street, but which flowers they hold has nothing to do with cyclist safety. Being on topic is not the same as supporting the claim.

C.why: You picked the choice that matches the topic, but it points the wrong way. More crashes after the lanes opened would weaken the claim, not support it.

D.why: This is about every city in the state, which is much broader than the claim. Statewide feelings could have many causes and don't show that Main Street in particular became safer.

stem: The passage ends with a claim. Which finding, if true, would make that claim more likely to be true?
stimulus: Several villages along the Varna River share a folktale about a fox who tricks a greedy miller into giving away his flour. Folklorist Mira Haddad has collected versions of the tale from each village. Haddad hypothesizes that the tale began in Ostrel, the village farthest upstream, and later spread downstream to the others.
choices: Storytellers in Ostrel today often perform the fox tale at the autumn harvest festival.
The oldest written version of the tale comes from the village farthest downstream.
Every village's version of the tale ends with the miller losing all of his flour.
The oldest written version of the tale was recorded in Ostrel, decades before any other.
explanation: The claim in your own words: the tale started in Ostrel and moved downstream from there. The key term is where it started. If Ostrel has the oldest record of the tale, decades ahead of the other villages, that points to Ostrel as the starting place. Asking what each choice says about the claim's key term is the step that unlocks real "which finding would support the hypothesis" questions.

A.why: This is an interesting fact about Ostrel and the tale, but it describes how the tale is told today. It says nothing about where the tale first began.

B.why: This puts the oldest version at the wrong end of the river. If the tale is oldest downstream, it suggests the tale spread upstream, which is the opposite of the hypothesis.

C.why: A shared ending shows the versions are related, but it doesn't show which village had the tale first. Reading it as evidence for Ostrel goes beyond what the fact shows.

stem: The passage ends with a claim. Which finding, if true, would make that claim more likely to be true?
stimulus: Paleobotanists studying a 50-million-year-old lake bed found that most of its fossil leaves have smooth edges rather than toothed ones. In forests today, smooth-edged leaves are most common where the climate is warm. Researcher Lena Park concludes that the climate around the ancient lake was warm when these leaves fell.
choices: The fossil leaves are unusually well preserved because the lake water held little oxygen.
Fossil pollen from the same layer comes from plants that today grow only in warm regions.
Fossil pollen from the same layer comes from plants that today grow only in cold regions.
The same lake bed also holds fossil leaves from several different species of fern.
explanation: The claim in your own words: it was warm around this lake when the leaves fell. The key term is "warm." Pollen from the same layer that comes only from warm-climate plants is a second, separate sign of warmth at the same place and time, so it makes the claim more likely. Real "if true, supports" questions often work like this: the right choice adds new evidence that points to the same conclusion.

A.why: This explains why the fossils survived, not what the climate was like. It is about the right leaves but has nothing to do with the claim about warmth.

C.why: This has the same structure as the right answer but points the other way. Cold-climate pollen would weaken the claim that the lake was warm.

D.why: Ferns at the site are an on-topic fact about the fossils, but nothing in the passage connects ferns to temperature. On its own, this tells you nothing about warmth.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?
stimulus: Many schools place hand-sanitizer stations at cafeteria entrances, hoping to slow the spread of colds and flu. Not every school can afford them, so the stations are found in some buildings but not in others. A public health researcher claims that putting sanitizer stations at cafeteria entrances reduces the number of days students miss school because of illness.
choices: Students at schools with the stations missed fewer days for illness than students at similar schools without them.
Most students at schools with the stations said in a survey that they liked having sanitizer near the cafeteria.
Laboratory tests show that alcohol-based sanitizer kills many common germs within thirty seconds of being applied.
Students at schools with the stations missed about as many days for illness as students at similar schools without them.
explanation: First put the claim in one sentence: the stations lead to fewer sick days. The key term is 'fewer sick days', so the finding you need has to compare sick days with and without the stations. Choice A does exactly that. Schools that are alike except for the stations, and the schools with stations have fewer absences. If A were true, you would believe the claim more. This is the basic move behind every 'which finding, if true, would support' question: find the claim's key term, then pick the finding that speaks to that term directly.

B.why: This is the trap the question is built around. It's on topic (same stations, same cafeterias) but it's about whether students like the stations, not whether students get sick less. Liking something is not the same as missing fewer school days, so the claim's actual point is left untouched.

C.why: This supports a broader idea, that sanitizer kills germs, not the specific claim that the stations cut sick days among students. Killing germs in a lab doesn't show that students actually use the stations or end up missing less school. You picked a fact that sounds like it leads to the claim but doesn't establish it.

D.why: This is the right kind of comparison pointing the wrong way. If sick days were the same with and without the stations, that would weaken the claim. Before you read the choices, decide which way the result has to go: fewer sick days with the stations.
